title: Image-based table recognition: data, model, and evaluation
research_question: How can complex tables in document images be converted into structured machine-readable representations while jointly recognizing table structure and cell content and evaluating both types of error appropriately?
methodology: The authors automatically construct PubTabNet by matching table regions in PDF articles from the PubMed Central Open Access collection with corresponding structured XML and converting the matched tables to images and curated HTML annotations. They propose an encoder-dual-decoder architecture with a ResNet-18 visual encoder, an attention-based LSTM structure decoder, and a separate attention-based LSTM cell-content decoder whose operation is guided by the structure decoder. They also introduce Tree-Edit-Distance-based Similarity, or TEDS, and compare EDD with PDF extraction tools and the WYGIWYS image-to-markup model, followed by error analysis and evaluation on a separate synthetic table dataset.

key_findings.finding: PubTabNet contains about 568,000 table images paired with structured HTML and provides large-scale supervision for both table structure and cell content recognition.

TEDS reacts more appropriately than the adjacency-relation metric to multi-hop cell shifts and graded OCR errors because it evaluates the complete table tree and uses content-sensitive substitution costs.
EDD achieved 88.3% average TEDS on the PubTabNet test set, compared with 78.6% for WYGIWYS, an absolute improvement of 9.7 percentage points.
EDD obtained 91.2% TEDS on simple tables and 85.4% on complex tables, and its advantage over WYGIWYS was slightly larger for complex tables.
On the separate synthetic benchmark, EDD achieved at least 99.7% TEDS in each of four table categories and higher exact-match rates than TIES in every category.
The PubTabNet version described in the paper did not contain table-cell coordinates, so its structured output could not directly ground recognized cells back to precise image regions.

limitations: The PubTabNet version evaluated in the paper does not provide coordinates for individual table cells, limiting precise source-region grounding.
EDD assumes that an accurately localized table image has already been supplied rather than performing table detection and recognition end to end.
Performance decreases as tables become larger, which the authors attribute mainly to stronger image downsampling when inputs are rescaled for batching.
Tables containing math or inline-formula nodes were filtered because those elements did not have consistent XML representations.
Training used only the subset of training samples satisfying image-size and sequence-length limits rather than the entire PubTabNet training set.
The core EDD model source code was not released because of legal constraints, although code for the TEDS metric and the dataset were released.
raw_claims: PubTabNet was generated by matching PDF table regions with corresponding XML table representations.
The dataset contains roughly 568,000 table images with HTML annotations.
EDD separates table-structure generation from cell-content recognition while allowing the structure decoder to guide cell recognition.
TEDS evaluates HTML tables as trees and incorporates cell-content edit similarity.
EDD scored 88.3% average TEDS over the PubTabNet test set.
WYGIWYS scored 78.6% average TEDS on the same test set.
Both EDD and WYGIWYS lose accuracy as table size increases.
EDD produced at least 99.7% TEDS in each category of the synthetic generalization experiment.
The original PubTabNet annotations described in the paper lacked cell coordinates.
The recognition model assumes that the table has already been accurately localized in the source document.
